paragraphs: 17 After Abram returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley).
18 Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine—since he was priest of God Most High — 19 and he blessed Abram and said:
“Blessed be Abram by God Most High,
20 and blessed be God Most High,
who has delivered your enemies into your hand.”
Then Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything.
21 The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself.”

22 But Abram replied to the king of Sodom, “I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, 23 that I will not accept even a thread, or a strap of a sandal, or anything that belongs to you, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’ 24 I will accept nothing but what my men have eaten and the share for the men who went with me—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. They may take their portion.”

context_lines: Two kings meet Abram after the rescue. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses him. His blessing credits God, the Creator of heaven and earth, with delivering Abram's enemies into his hand. Abram responds by giving Melchizedek a tenth of everything.

The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods if he will return the people. Abram refuses to let this king claim to have made him rich. He has sworn to the LORD, using the same title for God that Melchizedek used. His refusal makes his dependence clear: he will honor God as the source of his future rather than take wealth on terms that obscure that dependence.

Abram distinguishes his own decision from what belongs to others. He allows for what the men have eaten and for his allies to receive their shares. His personal refusal is not presented as a command that every other participant must refuse the same things. The scene holds together worship, gratitude, and care about the source of his wealth.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly recognize Melchizedek as a king-priest who honors God and blesses Abram. The Catholic [Catechism, 58](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_two/article_1/ii_the_stages_of_revelation.index.html), describes him as an earlier figure pointing to Christ. **Where do readings differ?** His identity has prompted several proposals. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 14:18](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) record both an identification with Shem and the view that this was an appearance of the Son of God, while declining to decide where Scripture does not expressly identify him.

The bread and wine are also given different emphases. [Wesley's notes](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) describe refreshment for Abram and his men. The Catholic Church's [Catechism, 1333](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_one/article_3/iii_the_eucharist_in_the_economy_of_salvation.index.html), also sees Melchizedek's gift as an earlier picture of the Church's offering in the Eucharist, or Lord's Supper. That reading connects the gift with the Church's later worship.
current_position_lines: Our Who Shepherds the Church? study draws from Melchizedek's appearance and Hebrews 7 to explain Christ's permanent priesthood. Because Jesus lives forever and intercedes for His people, they can draw near to God through Him. The study concludes that church leaders serve by teaching and caring for believers, rather than becoming an additional priestly class standing between them and God.
god_plan_lines: [Hebrews 7:1–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/7.htm) explicitly takes up this meeting. It explains Melchizedek's titles in terms of righteousness and peace, points to his blessing of Abraham and receipt of the tenth, and uses his priesthood to show a pattern greater than the later line of Levi. The brief Genesis account becomes important precisely because a priest of God appears before that later priesthood is established.

[Hebrews 7:20–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/7.htm) brings the connection to Jesus: His priesthood is confirmed by God's oath, He continues forever, and He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him. The earlier king-priest helps us understand the lasting priesthood of Christ. The hope is a living Savior whose help does not end with the death of another human priest.
